narrative: The model estimated a 75% chance that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it judged failure to be substantially more likely than success; because law-school admission here depends on that prediction, your application was rejected. The denial was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, far below the average of about the sixth decile among accepted students, and this factor pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other. Your first-year standing was the next most influential: third decile versus an accepted-student average of sixth decile, again pushing toward failure. Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most important factor; it was slightly above the accepted average of about 37, so it pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the two academic-standing signals. To move forward, ask admissions whether they will reconsider in light of any later improvement, and focus on strengthening your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate/graduate program. Retake the LSAT only if practice scores show a clear increase, apply to a balanced set of schools, and build a concrete bar-prep and study-support plan you can present as evidence of readiness.
